phonemes.text: In October 1936, an American magazine announced the result of the largest opinion poll ever taken.
phonemes.ipa: ɪn ɑːktˈoʊbɚ nˈaɪntiːnhˈʌndɹɪd θˈɜːɾi sˈɪks ɐn ɐmˈɛɹɪkən mˌæɡɐzˈiːn ɐnˈaʊnst ðə ɹɪzˈʌlt ʌvðə lˈɑːɹdʒɪst əpˈɪniən pˈoʊl ˈɛvɚ tˈeɪkən

phonemes.text: Two million four hundred thousand ballots, returned by mail.

phonemes.text: Its prediction: Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, fifty-seven to forty-three.
phonemes.ipa: ɪts pɹɪdˈɪkʃən ˈælf lˈændən wʊd bˈiːt fɹˈæŋklɪn ɹˈoʊzəvˌɛlt fˈɪftisˈɛvən tə fˈɔːɹɾiθɹˈiː

phonemes.text: Three weeks later Roosevelt won forty-six of forty-eight states.
phonemes.ipa: θɹˈiː wˈiːks lˈeɪɾɚ ɹˈoʊzəvˌɛlt wˈʌn fˈɔːɹɾisˈɪks ʌv fˈɔːɹɾiˈeɪt stˈeɪts

phonemes.text: This is the story of how the biggest poll in history got it backwards, and why a much smaller one got it right.
phonemes.ipa: ðɪs ɪz ðə stˈɔːɹi ʌv hˌaʊ ðə bˈɪɡɪst pˈoʊl ɪn hˈɪstɚɹi ɡɑːt ɪt bˈækwɚdz ænd wˌaɪ ɐ mˈʌtʃ smˈɔːlɚ wˈʌn ɡɑːt ɪt ɹˈaɪt

phonemes.text: The Literary Digest had called every presidential election since 1916.
phonemes.ipa: ðə lˈɪɾɚɹˌɛɹi daɪdʒˈɛst hæd kˈɔːld ˈɛvɹi pɹˌɛzɪdˈɛnʃəl ᵻlˈɛkʃən sˈɪns nˈaɪntiːnhˈʌndɹɪd sˈɪkstiːn

phonemes.text: Its method was scale.
phonemes.ipa: ɪts mˈɛθəd wʌz skˈeɪl

phonemes.text: It mailed ten million ballots, to names taken from telephone directories, automobile registrations and its own subscriber lists.
phonemes.ipa: ɪt mˈeɪld tˈɛn mˈɪliən bˈæləts tə nˈeɪmz tˈeɪkən fɹʌm tˈɛlᵻfˌoʊn dᵻɹˈɛktɚɹiz ˈɔːɾəməbˌiəl ɹˌɛdʒɪstɹˈeɪʃənz ænd ɪts ˈoʊn səbskɹˈaɪbɚ lˈɪsts

phonemes.text: About twenty-four percent came back.
phonemes.ipa: ɐbˌaʊt twˈɛntifˈɔːɹ pɚsˈɛnt kˈeɪm bˈæk

phonemes.text: Two point four million is an enormous sample.
phonemes.ipa: tˈuː pˈɔɪnt fˈɔːɹ mˈɪliən ɪz ɐn ɪnˈɔːɹməs sˈæmpəl

phonemes.text: It was also the wrong one, twice over.
phonemes.ipa: ɪt wʌz ˈɔːlsoʊ ðə ɹˈɔŋ wˈʌn twˈaɪs ˈoʊvɚ

phonemes.text: Here are the three numbers side by side.
phonemes.ipa: hˈɪɹ ɑːɹ ðə θɹˈiː nˈʌmbɚz sˈaɪd baɪ sˈaɪd

phonemes.text: The Digest, with two point four million ballots: Landon fifty-seven.
phonemes.ipa: ðə dˈaɪdʒɛst wɪð tˈuː pˈɔɪnt fˈɔːɹ mˈɪliən bˈæləts lˈændən fˈɪftisˈɛvən

phonemes.text: George Gallup, a young pollster with roughly fifty thousand interviews, chosen to mirror the population by region, income and sex: Roosevelt fifty-six.

phonemes.text: The election: Roosevelt about sixty-two to thirty-eight.
phonemes.ipa: ðɪ ᵻlˈɛkʃən ɹˈoʊzəvˌɛlt ɐbˌaʊt sˈɪkstitˈuː tə θˈɜːɾiˈeɪt

phonemes.text: The small sample was close.
phonemes.ipa: ðə smˈɔːl sˈæmpəl wʌz klˈoʊs

phonemes.text: The huge one was off by nineteen points.
phonemes.ipa: ðə hjˈuːdʒ wˈʌn wʌz ˈɔf baɪ nˈaɪntiːn pˈɔɪnts

phonemes.text: The first problem was who received a ballot.
phonemes.ipa: ðə fˈɜːst pɹˈɑːbləm wʌz hˌuː ɹᵻsˈiːvd ɐ bˈælət

phonemes.text: In 1936, in the middle of the Depression, owning a telephone or a car marked you as better off than most voters, and better-off voters leaned Republican.
phonemes.ipa: ɪn nˈaɪntiːnhˈʌndɹɪd θˈɜːɾi sˈɪks ɪnðə mˈɪdəl ʌvðə dᵻpɹˈɛʃən ˈoʊnɪŋ ɐ tˈɛlᵻfˌoʊn ɔːɹ ɐ kˈɑːɹ mˈɑːɹkt juː æz bˈɛɾɚɹ ˈɔf ðɐn mˈoʊst vˈoʊɾɚz ænd bˈɛɾɚɹˈɔf vˈoʊɾɚz lˈiːnd ɹᵻpˈʌblɪkən

phonemes.text: The list itself tilted toward Landon.
phonemes.ipa: ðə lˈɪst ɪtsˈɛlf tˈɪltᵻd təwˈɔːɹd lˈændən

phonemes.text: The second problem was who bothered to reply.
phonemes.ipa: ðə sˈɛkənd pɹˈɑːbləm wʌz hˌuː bˈɑːðɚd tə ɹᵻplˈaɪ

phonemes.text: Only one in four did.
phonemes.ipa: ˈoʊnli wˈʌn ɪn fˈɔːɹ dˈɪd

phonemes.text: In 1937 Gallup asked people whether they had received a Digest ballot and whether they had returned it.
phonemes.ipa: ɪn nˈaɪntiːnhˈʌndɹɪd θˈɜːɾi sˈɛvən ɡˈælʌp ˈæskt pˈiːpəl wˈɛðɚ ðeɪ hæd ɹᵻsˈiːvd ɐ dˈaɪdʒɛst bˈælət ænd wˈɛðɚ ðeɪ hæd ɹᵻtˈɜːnd ɪt

phonemes.text: Roosevelt supporters on the list had been less likely to send it back.
phonemes.ipa: ɹˈoʊzəvˌɛlt səpˈɔːɹɾɚz ɔnðə lˈɪst hɐdbɪn lˈɛs lˈaɪkli tə sˈɛnd ɪt bˈæk

phonemes.text: In 1988 the political scientist Peverill Squire re-analysed that survey and concluded that both biases were real, and that the failure to respond was the larger one.
phonemes.ipa: ɪn nˈaɪntiːnhˈʌndɹɪd ˈeɪɾi ˈeɪt ðə pəlˈɪɾɪkəl sˈaɪəntɪst pˈɛvɚɹˌɪl skwˈaɪɚ ɹˌiːˈænɐlˌaɪzd ðæt sˈɜːveɪ ænd kəŋklˈuːdᵻd ðæt bˈoʊθ bˈaɪəsᵻz wɜː ɹˈiːəl ænd ðætðə fˈeɪlɪɹ tə ɹᵻspˈɑːnd wʌzðə lˈɑːɹdʒɚ wˌʌn

phonemes.text: This is the lesson that survived.
phonemes.ipa: ðɪs ɪz ðə lˈɛsən ðæt sɚvˈaɪvd

phonemes.text: A biased sample does not get more accurate as it grows.
phonemes.ipa: ɐ bˈaɪəst sˈæmpəl dʌznˌɑːt ɡɛt mˈɔːɹ ˈækjʊɹət æz ɪt ɡɹˈoʊz

phonemes.text: It gets more confident.
phonemes.ipa: ɪt ɡˈɛts mˈɔːɹ kˈɑːnfɪdənt

phonemes.text: Two point four million ballots gave the Digest a precise estimate of the wrong population.
phonemes.ipa: tˈuː pˈɔɪnt fˈɔːɹ mˈɪliən bˈæləts ɡˈeɪv ðə dˈaɪdʒɛst ɐ pɹɪsˈaɪs ˈɛstᵻmət ʌvðə ɹˈɔŋ pˌɑːpjʊlˈeɪʃən

phonemes.text: The Literary Digest folded within two years.
phonemes.ipa: ðə lˈɪɾɚɹˌɛɹi daɪdʒˈɛst fˈoʊldᵻd wɪðˌɪn tˈuː jˈɪɹz

phonemes.text: Gallup's approach, small samples designed to look like the country, became the standard.
